meta.source: Curated generic US single-family curbside guidance, compiled from EPA and municipal program rules. Educational only - always check your local program.

regionNotes.us-ca-sf: San Francisco uses the three-cart system (blue recycling, green compost, black landfill) and composting of food soiled paper is mandatory.
regionNotes.us-ny-nyc: NYC DSNY separates organics (brown bin) from metal/glass/plastic/paper recycling; Electronics are banned from curbside trash.

clean.reasoning: Clean corrugated cardboard is widely recyclable. Flatten it and keep it dry.

contaminated.reasoning: Grease and cheese soaked into cardboard cannot be filtered out during paper recycling — it ruins the whole batch. Torn clean lids can still be recycled.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Food-soiled paper goes to landfill or compost depending on your program; grease is the #1 recycling contaminant.

clean.reasoning: Empty, clean and dry PET/HDPE bottles are among the most valuable recyclables. Caps on or off per local program.

contaminated.reasoning: Rinse it out first — leftover liquid or food residue can contaminate other recyclables, but the bottle itself still recycles.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Liquids and food residue are the top cause of rejected recycling loads.

clean.reasoning: Aluminum is infinitely recyclable and recycles with a fraction of the energy of new metal.

contaminated.reasoning: Still recyclable — rinse to keep pests away. If it's half full, empty it first.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Aluminum and steel cans are accepted in virtually every US curbside program.

clean.reasoning: Glass is infinitely recyclable with no loss of quality.

contaminated.reasoning: Rinse it out. Labels can stay on. If broken, wrap safely — some programs don't take broken glass curbside.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Ceramics, Pyrex and window glass are NOT the same as container glass — they melt differently and ruin batches.

clean.reasoning: Most to-go cups are lined with polyethylene that standard paper mills can't process — even 'clean' ones. The plastic lid usually recycles; the sleeve is compostable.

contaminated.reasoning: Leftover coffee plus the plastic lining makes this a textbook landfill item. Lid: recycle if marked #5. Sleeve: compost.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Wishcycling poster child: cups FEEL like paper but are plastic-lined composite.

clean.reasoning: Batteries must never go in curbside bins — lithium ones ignite in trucks and sorting facilities. Take to a drop-off (many hardware and electronics stores accept them).

contaminated.reasoning: Damaged or swollen batteries are a serious fire risk — tape the terminals and take to a hazardous waste drop-off immediately.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Batteries are the leading cause of recycling facility fires.

clean.reasoning: Electronics contain recoverable precious metals AND toxic solder, mercury or lead. E-waste drop-off or retailer take-back beats the landfill every time.

contaminated.reasoning: Still e-waste — wipe your data first, then drop off at an e-waste collection point.

baseRules.ruleDetail: E-waste is banned from curbside trash in many jurisdictions.

clean.reasoning: Bags and film jam sorting machinery — never curbside. Store-drop-off bins (grocery stores) take clean, dry bags and film.

contaminated.reasoning: Dirty or wet film isn't accepted even at store drop-off bins.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Film plastics tangle in sorting equipment, shutting facilities down for hours.

clean.reasoning: Food scraps are compost gold — if your city has organics collection, they belong in the green/brown bin.

contaminated.reasoning: All food is compostable, but remove any packaging first. Meat and dairy rules vary by program.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Food in landfill generates methane, a greenhouse gas ~28x more potent than CO2.

clean.reasoning: Expanded polystyrene (#6 foam) is rarely accepted curbside — it shatters and contaminates everything. Some specialty drop-offs take it.

contaminated.reasoning: Food-soiled foam is definitely landfill.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Foam has the recycling arrows symbol but almost no program takes it.

clean.reasoning: Textiles belong in donation bins or textile recycling drop-offs — 85% of clothing ends up landfilled, mostly from wishcycling into donation bins unwearable.

contaminated.reasoning: Wet, moldy or contaminated textiles can't be donated or recycled.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Donate wearable, recycle unwearable-but-dry, landfill only the truly contaminated.

clean.reasoning: Clean, dry paper is core curbside recycling. Windows in envelopes are fine.

contaminated.reasoning: Wet, greasy or wax-coated paper can't be recycled — fibers won't separate.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Paper fibers break down permanently when soaked.

clean.reasoning: Grounds, paper filters and most tea bags (check for plastic mesh) are compostable.

contaminated.reasoning: Even used with milk residue, grounds and filters compost fine in most programs.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Coffee grounds are nitrogen-rich compost material.

clean.reasoning: Rigid plastic containers (#1, #2, #5) recycle in most programs once rinsed.

contaminated.reasoning: Grease-soaked containers are too contaminated — a quick rinse is the difference between recycled and landfilled.

baseRules.ruleDetail: One greasy container can contaminate a bale of recyclables.

clean.reasoning: Paperboard boxes recycle — remove the plastic liner bag first.

contaminated.reasoning: If the box is grease-stained (frozen food boxes have coatings), it can't recycle.

baseRules.ruleDetail: The plastic liner bag inside goes to store drop-off with bags.

clean.reasoning: CFLs contain mercury — take to hazardous waste drop-off. LEDs contain electronics and belong in e-waste. Incandescents: trash.

contaminated.reasoning: A broken CFL releases mercury vapor — seal it in a container, don't vacuum, take to hazmat.

baseRules.ruleDetail: CFL → hazmat. LED → e-waste. Incandescent → landfill.

clean.reasoning: Liquid paint (oil-based) is household hazardous waste. Latex paint can be dried out with cat litter and trashed where programs allow — or better, donated.

contaminated.reasoning: Take to a paint or hazmat drop-off — many paint retailers participate in take-back programs.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Fully dried latex paint is often landfill-safe; liquid paint never is.

clean.reasoning: Never flush or bin meds — take to pharmacy take-back kiosks. FDA guidance allows trashing (mixed with coffee grounds) only when no take-back exists.

contaminated.reasoning: Same rule — pharmacy take-back.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Meds contaminate waterways; take-back is always first choice.

clean.reasoning: Too small for sorting equipment — shredded paper falls through machinery. Compost it (if not glossy) or bag separately where accepted.

contaminated.reasoning: Contaminated shreds: landfill.

baseRules.ruleDetail: Anything smaller than a credit card falls through sorting screens.

clean.reasoning: Metallized plastic film (crinkly, shiny) can't recycle curbside. Terracycle-style specialty programs exist.

contaminated.reasoning: Crumb-filled wrappers: landfill, no debate.

baseRules.ruleDetail: If it crinkles and springs back, it's metallized film — landfill.

contaminated.reasoning: San Francisco's green compost cart takes greasy pizza boxes — food-soiled paper composts here by law.

clean.reasoning: Mandatory composting in SF — all food scraps go in the green cart.
SF accepts paper cups in the green compost cart (lined cups break down in commercial composting).
NYC bans electronics from trash entirely — use DSNY e-waste drop-off or SAFE Disposal events.
NYC curbside organics collection is citywide — food scraps go in the brown bin.
